title: Multi-tenant patterns: tenant column, schema per tenant, database per tenant, and RLS
summary: Tenants can share tables (a tenant_id column), share a database (a schema each) or get a database each. With shared tables, put tenant_id into every key and foreign key, and let row-level security add the tenant filter that a query might forget.

examples.title: Shared tables: tenant_id in every key and every foreign key

annotations.note: projects keeps a global id as its primary key and also declares UNIQUE (tenant_id, id). That looks redundant, but a foreign key can only reference a unique constraint on exactly its columns, and (tenant_id, id) is the pair children must match.
The naive foreign key checks that project 10 exists somewhere. Güney's requirement now sits in Kuzey's project, and every join from it puts Kuzey's data on Güney's pages.
Codes are unique per tenant, so both tenants have a REQ-1. A plain UNIQUE (code) would let one customer's naming block another's, and the duplicate key error would tell them the other code exists.

The composite foreign key puts the tenant into the reference: a requirement's project must belong to the requirement's tenant. Do the same in every child table, and the tenant boundary becomes a property of the schema instead of each query.
Indexes lead with tenant_id, because every query filters by it. This one also serves the foreign key when projects are deleted.

Column tenancy's weak spot: isolation is a WHERE clause every query has to remember. The second query stands for any admin page, report or bug: both tenants in one result, and no error. Example 3 moves the filter into the database.
(2, 10) matches no row in projects: SQLSTATE 23503. The naive table accepted the same row on line 19.

examples.title: Schema per tenant: search_path does the isolation, migrations multiply

annotations.note: Each tenant gets the same tables in its own schema. Isolation is name resolution: an unqualified requirements is one tenant's table, and there is no tenant_id to forget. StackLab runs every SQL example the same way, in a throwaway schema on the search_path.

SET LOCAL lasts until the transaction ends. A plain SET would stay on the pooled connection and serve the next request, possibly another tenant's, from this schema. Behind a transaction-mode pooler, transaction-scoped settings are the only safe kind.
Anything across tenants (billing, usage dashboards, support queries) becomes a UNION over every schema, generated by code that knows the list of schemas.
A migration is now one per tenant, and each can fail on its own. The catalog query is the drift check you'll need: tenant_kuzey has 3 columns, tenant_guney 2.
The new code is deployed everywhere, and the tenant whose migration didn't run gets SQLSTATE 42703 while the others work. Every deploy becomes a fleet rollout.

examples.title: Row-level security: the database adds the tenant filter

annotations.note: The default takes the tenant from the session setting, so inserts don't name it. current_setting without a second argument raises an error when the setting doesn't exist (SQLSTATE 42704): a request that forgot to set its tenant fails instead of seeing everything.

ENABLE turns policies on for everyone except superusers, BYPASSRLS roles and the table's owner. The role running this script owns the table, as an application role that runs its own migrations would, so FORCE is what makes the policy apply to it. Enabled with no policy at all, the table shows no rows (default deny).

One policy for every command. USING filters the rows that SELECT, UPDATE and DELETE can see; without a WITH CHECK clause the same expression also checks the rows INSERT and UPDATE write. The RLS lesson in the security module covers per-command policies.
Superusers and roles with BYPASSRLS ignore every policy, FORCE or not. Check the application's role once, in a test; playground has neither attribute.

set_config(name, value, true) is SET LOCAL as a function: it ends with the transaction, and unlike SET it accepts a query parameter, so the tenant id travels as $1 rather than spliced into SQL text. Custom setting names need a dot: PostgreSQL accepts any two-part name.
Tenant 2 sees only its own row, though the query has no WHERE. The policy applies to every query on the table, including ones written by someone who never heard of tenants.
Tenant 1's row is invisible, so the UPDATE matches nothing: UPDATE 0, no error. Policies filter silently on read; they raise errors only for rows being written.
tenant_id came from the column default, that is from the setting, so the new row belongs to tenant 2.

A row for tenant 1 fails the policy's check: SQLSTATE 42501. Note what RLS doesn't hide: unique and foreign key checks bypass policies, so inserting id 1 here would fail with a duplicate key and reveal that the row exists. Keys that include tenant_id avoid that leak.

use_cases: Shared tables with tenant_id and RLS: SaaS with many small tenants, such as a hosted TraceLite; the usual default
Schema per tenant: tens to a few hundred tenants that need per-tenant restore, customization or contractual separation

Database per tenant: a few large or regulated tenants that need their own backups, resource limits, versions or server; for example to keep a tenant's personal data in Turkey, where KVKK Article 9 regulates transfers abroad
Offboarding and erasure requests: DELETE ... WHERE tenant_id = $1 across tables, DROP SCHEMA ... CASCADE, or DROP DATABASE
strengths: With shared tables, composite foreign keys make cross-tenant references impossible in the schema, not just unlikely in the code
RLS covers every query on the table, including reports and ad-hoc SQL run as the app role, unlike Hibernate filters or Rails default scopes, which only cover ORM queries
Schema tenancy needs no tenant_id in queries, and one tenant can be dumped or restored with standard tools (pg_dump --schema)
Database tenancy gives the strongest boundary: separate connections, privileges, backups and resource limits per tenant
weaknesses: Shared tables without RLS depend on every query remembering WHERE tenant_id, and the one that forgets leaks without an error
Schema tenancy multiplies tables, indexes and migrations by the number of tenants, and cross-tenant reports need a UNION per schema
Database tenancy needs a connection pool per database, since a connection is bound to one database, and cross-tenant queries need postgres_fdw or an export
RLS adds a predicate to every query, doesn't hide anything from unique and foreign key checks, and is skipped by superusers, BYPASSRLS roles and, without FORCE, the owner

pitfalls.title: Session-level SET behind a connection pool
pitfalls.detail: A plain SET stays on the connection after the request, and the pool hands that connection to the next request. Set the tenant per transaction.

pitfalls.title: Foreign keys that leave out tenant_id
pitfalls.detail: A reference by id alone checks existence, not ownership, so one tenant's row can point at another's.
pitfalls.good: FOREIGN KEY (tenant_id, project_id) REFERENCES projects (tenant_id, id)

pitfalls.title: ENABLE without FORCE
pitfalls.detail: If the application connects as the table's owner, which is common when it runs its own migrations, ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY alone protects nothing. Use separate owner and application roles (the roles lesson), and FORCE anyway.

pitfalls.title: An empty setting is not a missing one
pitfalls.detail: Once a session has used app.tenant, the setting keeps existing with an empty value after the transaction ends, so current_setting('app.tenant', true) returns '' rather than NULL. Make sure both NULL and '' match no rows, and never coalesce to a default tenant.

pitfalls.title: Global unique keys under RLS
pitfalls.detail: Unique and foreign key checks bypass policies, so a duplicate key error can confirm that another tenant's row exists. Put tenant_id into unique keys over tenant data.

quiz.q: requirements has FOREIGN KEY (project_id) REFERENCES projects (id), and both tables have tenant_id. What stops tenant 2's requirement from pointing at tenant 1's project?
quiz.why: The foreign key only checks that the project exists. Referencing (tenant_id, id) makes ownership part of the check.

quiz.q: The application connects as the table's owner. RLS is enabled with a tenant policy but not forced. What do its queries see?
options: All rows: the owner bypasses RLS
quiz.why: Table owners bypass row security unless the table has FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY.

quiz.q: Why call set_config('app.tenant', $1, true) inside each transaction instead of running SET app.tenant once per connection?
options: The local setting ends with the transaction, so a pooled connection can't carry one tenant's id into another request
quiz.why: A session-level SET outlives the request on a pooled connection. A transaction-local setting is gone at COMMIT or ROLLBACK, and set_config also takes the value as a parameter.

quiz.q: With app.tenant = 2 and the tenant_isolation policy, `UPDATE requirements SET code = 'X' WHERE id = 1` targets tenant 1's row. What happens?
quiz.why: USING hides the row, so the UPDATE finds nothing to change. Errors come only from rows being written that fail the check.

further_reading.title: PostgreSQL docs: Configuration Settings Functions (set_config, current_setting)

body:
## Concept

A multi-tenant application serves many customers (tenants) from one deployment. The
database has to keep their data apart, and there are three places to draw the line:

- **Shared tables, tenant column**: every table has `tenant_id`. Cheapest and densest;
  one schema, one migration, one pool. Isolation is a predicate on every query, which
  you either write yourself or let row-level security add.
- **Schema per tenant**: the same tables in a schema per tenant, chosen per request
  with `search_path`. Isolation is name resolution; the cost is N copies of every
  table, index and migration.
- **Database per tenant**: a database (or server) each. Isolation is the connection
  itself. Not demonstrated here: the playground role can't create databases, which is
  itself an example of the least privilege an application role should have.

**Row-level security (RLS)** is the database's half of the tenant-column design: a
policy such as `tenant_id = current_setting('app.tenant')::int` is added to every query
on the table, so a query that forgets the tenant still sees only one.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **Java/Hibernate:** Hibernate's multi-tenancy offers the same three strategies: a
  separate database, a separate schema, or a discriminator column (`@TenantId` in
  Hibernate 6). Its filters only cover queries Hibernate runs; RLS also covers native
  queries, reports and psql.
- **Rails:** acts_as_tenant (column) and Apartment (schema per tenant) are the two
  well-known gems; both work at the ORM level.
- **Go:** there is no framework to do this for you, which keeps it visible. A
  middleware resolves the tenant from the authenticated request and puts it into the
  `context.Context`; the store's `WithTx` helper begins the transaction and runs
  `SELECT set_config('app.tenant', $1, true)` before anything else.
- **Node:** the tenant often lives in `AsyncLocalStorage` for the duration of a
  request. The database setting has to have exactly that lifetime, which is why it is
  transaction-local and not set once per pooled connection.

## How it works

One request, in the tenant-column design with RLS:

1. Authenticate and resolve the tenant (never from a client-supplied header alone).
2. `BEGIN`, then `SELECT set_config('app.tenant', $1, true)`.
3. Run the queries. Policies filter what they read and check what they write; column
   defaults fill `tenant_id` on insert.
4. `COMMIT` or `ROLLBACK`. The setting is gone, and the connection goes back to the
   pool clean.

If step 2 is skipped, `current_setting('app.tenant')` raises an error on a fresh
connection; on a connection that has used the setting before, it returns an empty
string, which fails the `::int` cast. Either way the request fails rather than leaking.

## Design notes

Start with shared tables, `tenant_id` in every table, and RLS as defence in depth:

- Put `tenant_id` first in primary keys or alongside them in UNIQUE constraints, in
  every foreign key, and first in indexes. Cross-tenant references then become
  impossible, and every tenant-scoped query has an index to narrow on.
- Separate the role that owns the tables (runs migrations) from the role the
  application uses, give the application role neither superuser nor `BYPASSRLS`, and
  still `FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY`.
- Write one integration test per table that sets tenant A and asserts that tenant B's
  rows are invisible and unwritable.

Move to a schema or a database per tenant when a tenant needs something shared tables
can't give: its own restore point, its own resource limits, contractual or legal
separation, or a location. Having `tenant_id` in every key makes that move a copy of
the rows `WHERE tenant_id = $1`, not a redesign.

Offboarding is part of the design. Under KVKK, a customer that leaves may be owed
erasure of the personal data you processed for them: with shared tables that's a
`DELETE` per table, children first or by `ON DELETE CASCADE` from `tenants`; with
schemas a `DROP SCHEMA ... CASCADE`; with databases a `DROP DATABASE`. Backups and
history tables (temporal lesson) hold copies too.
